title: He Backed His Wife's Biryani in 1957. Now It Is Worth Rs 1,000 Crore
excerpt: Nagasamy Naidu opened a four-seater hotel in Dindigul around his wife's unique biryani. Dindigul Thalappakatti grew into a 100-plus outlet chain now reported to be seeking a valuation of around Rs 1,000 crore.
body:
• Dindigul Thalappakatti began in 1957 when Nagasamy Naidu, who had started with a betel nut shop, opened a small four-seater hotel in Dindigul built around his wife's unique style of biryani.
  • The brand's own history says her recipes — using short-grain seeraga samba rice and a special spice blend — are what turned a local eatery into a South Indian institution.
  • Decades later, the chain is reported to be seeking a valuation of around Rs 1,000 crore as majority owner CX Partners prepares an exit, up from a Rs 860 crore valuation in its 2021 funding round.
  • Thalappakatti Hotels reported revenue of Rs 406.2 crore in FY25, up from Rs 340.3 crore a year earlier, with profit of Rs 7.3 crore, according to filings cited in the reports.

It started with a betel nut shop, a four-seater hotel, and a husband's belief in his wife's cooking. In 1957, Nagasamy Naidu founded the Anandha Vilas Biriyani Hotel in Dindigul, Tamil Nadu — the eatery that would become Dindigul Thalappakatti, today one of India's best-known biryani chains. Decades later, the business built on his wife's biryani is reported to be worth around Rs 1,000 crore.

The brand tells the origin story plainly on its official history page: "Started as a Betel nut shop, Mr. Nagasamy Naidu took the chance of opening a small 4-seater hotel which made him realise that his wife's unique style of biriyani had potential to go places." Started by serving his locality, the page adds, the aroma brought in fans from neighbouring cities.

The wife's recipe at the centre

Accounts of the brand's history agree on the core detail: the recipes were specially curated by Naidu's wife, an amalgamation of herbs, spices, vegetables and meat. The biryani that carried the family name was made with superior-quality seeraga samba rice — the short-grain variety the brand calls Parakkum Sittu — and meat from cattle markets at Kannivadi and Paramathi. Unlike basmati, the brand notes, seeraga samba has little taste of its own, so it absorbs the flavours of the spices completely. Naidu also created Dalcha, a combination dish served with the biryani, made with mutton bones and vegetables including brinjal and potato.

Naidu himself became the brand. He always wore a traditional turban — a thalapa — which became synonymous with his cooking, earning him the nickname "Thalappakatti Naidu." That nickname eventually became the name of the restaurants. The brand says his cooking style and secrets were passed down through family members and are still followed, which it credits for keeping the Thalappakatti taste unchanged across generations. In South India, it notes, the word "Thalappakatti" itself came to refer to high-quality biryani.

From one outlet in Dindigul to a national chain

For decades the business remained rooted in Dindigul before expanding across South India and beyond. By 2021 the brand operated over 85 restaurants and cloud kitchens globally, and more recent reports put the chain at over 100 outlets across India, with a strong concentration in the southern states. The business is now led by third-generation leader Nagasamy Dhanabalan, Naidu's grandson, and industry assessments cited in earlier coverage have described Dindigul Thalappakatti as the largest biryani brand in India in the organised biryani market.

How the Rs 1,000 crore figure is reported

The Rs 1,000 crore number is a reported valuation being sought, not a closed sale price. According to reports of private equity firm CX Partners' planned exit, the firm — which bought a majority stake in Thalappakatti Hotels in October 2019 — is working with Advay Capital on a divestment that aims to value the chain at approximately Rs 1,000 crore, at roughly two to three times revenue. That would be up from about Rs 860 crore in the previous funding round.

The earlier steps are on the record. The Hindu BusinessLine reported in October 2021 that the brand raised growth capital led by Tree Line Investment Management, with the Havells Group family office among the investors, at a valuation of Rs 860 crore — up from Rs 450 crore when the CX Partners-led consortium picked up its majority stake in 2019, in what was then one of the largest investments in a local restaurant chain in India. The BusinessLine report said the 2021 capital was to fast-track growth across Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.

The financials behind the latest figure, as reported from Ministry of Corporate Affairs filings, show Thalappakatti Hotels' revenue from operations rising to Rs 406.2 crore in 2024-25 from Rs 340.3 crore the year before, with profit widening to Rs 7.3 crore from Rs 4.4 crore. The final structure of the CX Partners exit — a full divestment, possibly combining primary and secondary share purchases — will depend on the incoming investor. What is already clear is the arc: a wife's biryani, served first to a single locality in 1957, now anchors a chain that investors value in the region of Rs 1,000 crore.
